A work table that changes posture. Phasmos takes its name and its logic from the stick insect: an organism whose entire survival strategy rests on the ability to adapt its form to its context without changing what it fundamentally is. The table does the same.

The reference

The Phasmatidae family, commonly known as stick insects, are masters of structural mimicry. Their elongated bodies, articulated limbs, and capacity to hold any posture for long periods without losing stability made them an ideal formal reference for a piece of furniture designed around adaptability.

The specific species studied was Ctenomorpha chronus, chosen for the clarity of its joint structure and the range of positions its legs can assume while keeping the body level, elevated, or inclined.

Corpo
Elongated and thin, designed to imitate twigs. The table's top surface inherits this linearity: a long, narrow plane that reads as a single element regardless of the leg configuration beneath it.
Zampe
Long, thin, adapted for climbing. Each pair can be set at a different angle independently, enabling the insect to keep its body stable on uneven surfaces. The table's articulated legs follow the same principle.
Giunti
Spherical joints at the shoulder and knee of each leg allow multi-axis movement. The table's ball-and-socket connection points at the top and base of each leg reproduce this range directly.
Mimetismo
The insect blends into the environment not by changing colour but by changing shape. The table's three named postures follow this logic: each is a functional response to a different context of use, not a decorative variation.

The table

The top surface is a single dark glass panel running the full length of the frame. Below it, three pairs of articulated wooden legs connect to a central steel spine through ball-and-socket joints at two points each, top and base. Every joint can be locked at any angle within its range. The table has no fixed height, no fixed incline, and no fixed width between the leg pairs.

The design process moved from insect posture studies to schematic leg diagrams, then to joint mechanism sketches, and finally to the three named configurations. Each posture was derived from a real insect behaviour rather than invented as a product feature.

The three postures

Each posture takes its name from a stick insect behaviour. Each one corresponds to a specific use condition rather than a visual preference.

Posa a riposo

The standard configuration. All six legs at the same angle, the top surface horizontal at working height. Used for writing, drawing, or computer work. The insect equivalent is the resting stance on a flat branch: stable, symmetrical, undemanding.

Surface
Horizontal · standard height
Use
Writing · computer · dining

Posa estesa

The legs splay outward, lowering the top surface and widening the footprint. The table becomes a large low platform, suited to group work or large-scale projects. The stick insect does this to stabilise itself on wide, irregular surfaces.

Surface
Lowered · wide footprint
Use
Group work · large projects

Posa da mimesi

The front legs raise, the rear legs lower, inclining the surface toward the user. The table becomes an angled drawing board or reading stand, adapting its geometry to the posture of the person using it rather than asking them to adapt to it.

Surface
Inclined · ergonomic angle
Use
Drawing · reading · standing work

The process

The project began with a biological research phase on the Phasmatidae family, focusing specifically on joint morphology and the mechanics of postural change. The moodboard collected images of stick insects in different configurations and extracted from them a colour palette of ambers, greens, ochres, and greys that informed both the material choices and the finish of the final object.

From there the process moved through hand sketches of leg positions, schematic diagrams mapping insect pose to table configuration, 3D modelling in the three named postures, and technical drawing at full dimensions.

The course was Forme e Soluzioni Biologiche e Design, Università degli Studi Mediterranea di Reggio Calabria, Design L-4.
